5: A cotton mill set up by Japanese businessmen in Yangshupu, Shanghai. After victory in the War of Resistance in 1945 it was taken over by the state and renamed China Textile Construction Company No. 17 Cotton Mill. This later became the No. 17 State Cotton Mill, one of the largest textile mills in Shanghai. Many of the old workers had lived through the days of Japanese foremen. For them, “standing up” was something concrete. This is one reason they later expected so much of the factory Party committee, and were so deeply disappointed.
7: Wang Hongwen's wife, a worker at the No. 17 State Cotton Mill. After the Cultural Revolution she said Wang Hongwen “liked to poke his nose into other people's business.” In October 1976 Wang Hongwen sent a secretary to ask her for a divorce, so the family would not be dragged down with him. She said she would agree if she got the children. The paperwork was not finished when he was arrested.
10: Party general branch secretary of the Philosophy Department at Peking University. On May 25, 1966, she and six others put up a big-character poster at Peking University that named and criticized the university Party secretary Lu Ping and others. Mao Zedong ordered it broadcast nationwide, and this set off rebellion across the country. Nie later became one of the “Five Great Leaders” of the Beijing Red Guards. In 1983 she was sentenced to 17 years in prison.
11: first Marxist-Leninist big-character poster in the country
12: "The First Marxist-Leninist Big-Character Poster in the Country"
13: Mao Zedong's comment on Nie Yuanzi's poster. On the evening of June 1, 1966, Central People's Broadcasting Station read out the poster. The next day People's Daily printed it in full, with a commentator's article titled “Hail a Big-Character Poster at Peking University.” It sent the whole country a signal that the masses could openly criticize the Party organization in their own work unit. For people in the factories who had been pushed around, it was the first time in 17 years they had heard words like these come out of the loudspeaker.
15: Text written with a brush on large sheets of paper and posted in public places. It was the main way the masses expressed themselves in the Cultural Revolution. Whom you wrote about, whether you signed, and where you posted it could all decide your fate from then on. The 1975 Constitution wrote “speaking out freely, airing views fully, holding great debates, writing big-character posters” into its text. They were removed in 1980.
17: From 1961 Deng Tuo, Wu Han and Liao Mosha wrote a joint column of essays called “Notes from Three-Family Village” in Frontline, the journal of the Beijing Municipal Party Committee. In May 1966 the column was branded an “anti-Party, anti-socialist” black shop and criticized across the country. Early in the Cultural Revolution, posters in many work units first went after distant targets like this one. Nobody dared touch the leaders of their own unit.
19: In June 1966, while Mao Zedong was away from Beijing, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping ran the daily work of the center. They decided to send work teams into schools and factories to lead the movement. The work teams generally turned the movement against “ox-demons and snake-spirits” and against people who had criticized their Party committees. At the end of July Mao Zedong came back to Beijing, criticized the work teams for “suppressing the masses,” and ordered them out of the schools. After that, “opposing the work teams” became a source of legitimacy for the rebels. Two work teams came to the No. 17 State Cotton Mill. The one sent by the Textile Bureau on June 20 praised Wang Hongwen's big-character poster. The one sent by the Municipal Party Committee on July 20 no longer gave him important work.
21: A catch-all term in the Cultural Revolution for every kind of “class enemy.” It could be stretched without limit. Landlords, rich peasants, counterrevolutionaries, bad elements, rightists, and anyone with “historical problems” could all be counted in. Putting the weight of the movement on “sweeping away ox-demons and snake-spirits” usually meant that ordinary people were the ones persecuted, while those in power stayed safe.
24: In Chinese urban work units, everyone had a personnel dossier. The organization kept it, the person could not read it, and it followed them from job to job. It decided everything, from joining the Party and promotion to getting housing. Early in the Cultural Revolution, work teams and Party committees collected what people said and did, wrote it up and put it in their dossiers. These files were later called “black materials.” Demanding that black materials be destroyed was one of the rebels' most urgent demands in the fall and winter of 1966. Ten years later, the investigation of the “three kinds of people” used the same paper envelopes.
26: The “Decision of the CCP Central Committee Concerning the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution,” passed by the Eleventh Plenum of the Eighth Central Committee on August 8, 1966. It had sixteen points. It said the main target of the movement was “those power holders within the Party who are taking the capitalist road,” and it warned against labeling the masses as counterrevolutionaries. Rebels everywhere carried it as a protective charm.
28: Born in 1948, a student at the No. 17 State Cotton Mill vocational school. Early in the Cultural Revolution he brought Red Guards to get Wang Hongwen out of a siege, and he followed him from then on. He later became Wang Hongwen's personal secretary in Beijing. His memories are an important source on Wang Hongwen's private life, but most versions that circulate online have been rewritten.
30: The theoretical journal of the CCP Central Committee, run during the Cultural Revolution by Chen Boda and others. Together with People's Daily and PLA Daily it was known as the “two papers and one journal.” Its editorials often showed the latest intentions at the very top.
32: A phrase formally put forward in October 1966 by a Red Flag editorial and the Central Work Conference. It meant the early practice of sending in work teams and attacking the masses. Once something was labeled the “reactionary line,” people who had been persecuted could demand rehabilitation, and the cadres who had persecuted them had to make self-criticisms. This turn changed large numbers of grassroots rebels from “people who had been persecuted” into “people who were right.”
34: Mass organizations made up mainly of university and middle school students, from 1966 on. From August Mao Zedong received Red Guards at Tiananmen several times, and the nationwide “great linking up” began. Students rode trains for free and traveled around the country. Beijing students coming to Shanghai to link up were an important early push for the Shanghai worker rebels.
37: A worker at the No. 30 State Cotton Mill and a model worker. She was an early core member of the Workers' General Headquarters and later a secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. She was one of the highest-ranking Shanghai women workers of the Cultural Revolution. On August 21, 1982, the Shanghai Higher People's Court sentenced her to 17 years in prison. She was released in 1994 at the end of her sentence. Some sources give her birth year as 1935.
40: A worker at the No. 31 State Cotton Mill, named a Shanghai Five-Good Worker in 1965. Early in the Cultural Revolution he was branded anti-Party over a big-character poster. Angry, he rebelled, and he was one of the founders of the Workers' General Headquarters. He later sat on the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. After 1976 he was sentenced to 15 years for “counterrevolutionary crimes.” He came out of prison in 1991 and in his last years wrote a memoir, Ten Years Not a Dream. The title answers Xu Jingxian's Ten Years, One Dream.
42: An honorary title awarded in factories in the 1960s. It required being good in political thinking, completing tasks, keeping discipline, helping others, and study. The people chosen were usually the recognized activists of their workshop.
44: A political verdict. Once it was pinned on you, you could not hold your head up in your work unit, a record went into your dossier, and your family suffered too. Early in the Cultural Revolution many people who had only criticized their grassroots Party organization were given this label.
46: Studying the Selected Works of Mao Zedong. In the 1960s a campaign to “study Chairman Mao's writings” was pushed nationwide, and factory workshops commonly set up study groups. Criticizing a Party organization for not studying Mao's works seriously meant criticizing it from the most correct position there was. You could still be branded anti-Party for it.
49: A young worker at the Shanghai Glass Machinery Plant and one of the most active early leaders of the Workers' General Headquarters. People called him “Commander Pan,” and for a time he was better known than Wang Hongwen. In the Anting negotiations he was the main person talking with Zhang Chunqiao. After that he was pushed to the margins and investigated several times. He was not a Party member and had no record as a cadre. As the WGHQ was absorbed into the system, this became a fatal weakness.
50: Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters
52: The Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters, founded in November 1966, with Wang Hongwen as its main leader. It was the first citywide, cross-industry workers' rebel organization in the country to be openly backed by the Central Cultural Revolution Group. From 1967 it was gradually made part of the system, and its core members joined revolutionary committees at every level. It stayed active in Shanghai politics for a full ten years. After 1976 its members were investigated one by one, and many carried this identity for the rest of their lives.
55: Then mayor of Shanghai and a secretary of the Municipal Party Secretariat. He ran daily work while the first secretary, Chen Pixian, was on sick leave. Toward the Workers' General Headquarters he followed a policy of “no joining, no recognition, no support.” On December 23 he signed to recognize the Scarlet Guards, and two days later, at a rebel rally, he announced that the signature was void. He was overthrown after the January Storm of 1967 and died in 1976. In just over two months he signed for both factions and took both signatures back. That was the position of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee that winter.
56: no joining, no recognition, no support
58: The Shanghai Municipal Party Committee's stance toward the Workers' General Headquarters. The central rules at the time said workers could not link up across factories or form cross-industry organizations, and the Municipal Party Committee used this as its basis. To the rebels, this amounted to declaring them illegal.
61: Shanghai's main railway station at the time, and the start of the Shanghai-Nanjing line. In the early hours of November 10, workers from the Workers' General Headquarters squeezed onto northbound trains here.
63: A small town in Jiading County, Shanghai, and a small station on the Shanghai-Nanjing Railway, more than 30 kilometers from the city. This stretch was single-track. At 8:17 a.m. on November 10, 1966, slow train No. 602, carrying the workers heading north, was ordered onto a siding here, next to a coal yard. After that, people stood by the tracks waving caps and jackets to stop passing trains. This became known as the “Anting Incident.” Which trains were stopped, and for how long, is still told several ways. A month and a half later, the Scarlet Guards went north to petition and were stopped at Kunshan, near the next station.
66: The railway from Shanghai to Nanjing, at the time one of the busiest trunk lines in the country, linking to the Beijing-Shanghai line. There are three accounts of how long it was cut during the Anting Incident. A 1979 document from the dispatch office of the Shanghai Railway Sub-bureau says 31 hours 34 minutes. Ye Yonglie says 20 hours 21 minutes. Huang Jinhai says train No. 648, which was stopped, waited only twenty-some minutes. The dispatch document was written during the investigations, and the head of the dispatch office, Wang Yuxi, happened to be a leader of the Scarlet Guards. This is why Huang Jinhai did not trust it.
68: A cadre in the No. 17 State Cotton Mill security section, two years older than Wang Hongwen, and once on very good terms with him. In June 1966 he too wrote a big-character poster to the factory Party committee and went with Wang Hongwen to complain to the Textile Bureau. When the work team came, he decided it had been sent by the Party and went over to the other side. In October he set up a “Defense Team” and wrote an influential poster, “The Rebels in Our Factory.” On November 25 the No. 17 Mill Scarlet Guards were founded, four or five thousand strong, and he led them. After the Kangping Road Incident he was held in Tilanqiao for more than a month. When he was let out he cleared loom waste in the No. 2 spinning shop and was paraded with placards hung on his front and back. In 1969, when the No. 17 Mill Party committee was restored, three Party members in the whole mill did not vote for Wang Hongwen, and he was one of them. He was put under isolation and investigation for more than a month again. In 1972 his case was settled and he became a canteen manager. He never went back to the security section. He said later, “I was one of the earliest rebels too. But my rebellion and Wang Hongwen's were two different things.” He also said, “The higher Wang Hongwen climbed, the less I could make sense of it... I know what cards he holds.” See Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), chs. 10 and 14.
70: Secretary in the director's office of the Shanghai Railway Sub-bureau and one of the main leaders of the Scarlet Guards headquarters. On the night of the Anting Incident he and deputy director Li Dianyuan rushed to Anting and spent two hours trying to talk the people blocking the trains into stopping. In early December he gave a report on Wang Yuxi's behalf, calling for criticism of the Municipal Party Committee and closer unity with the rebels. The team leaders under him denounced this as a “capitulationist policy.” After the Kangping Road Incident he was locked up for ten months. In 1969 he was sent off to the Meishan steel base. See Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), chs. 10 and 13.
72: A conservative workers' organization. Its full name was the Shanghai Headquarters of the Workers' Scarlet Guards for Defending Mao Zedong Thought. According to Huang Jinhai, on November 19 Cao Diqiu received representatives of the conservative workers. On the 23rd they held a preparatory meeting in a meeting room of the Yangpu District Party Committee. Yang Shifa, head of the Organization Department of the Municipal Party Committee, backed them and gave them an office. On December 6 they held a founding rally in People's Square (Wikipedia gives November 26 as the founding date). At its peak it claimed 800,000 members. Most of its founders were leaders of the opposing faction in the same units that had founded the WGHQ. At No. 17 Mill it was Ma Ji. At the railway dispatch office it was Wang Yuxi. Its members were mostly Party and Youth League members, model workers and workshop activists. They truly believed they were defending the Party and production. They had also gained from the new China, and they believed that following the Party committee would not do them wrong. On December 30 they were scattered at Kangping Road. After that they were banned across the city, and many members were arrested and struggled against.
75: Mao Zedong's longtime secretary, head of the Central Cultural Revolution Group, and editor-in-chief of Red Flag. During the Anting Incident he wrote a telegram by hand urging the workers to go back to Shanghai, saying “solve problems where you are.” Mao Zedong, Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao later rejected this telegram. He fell after the Lushan Conference of 1970.
78: A secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Secretariat and deputy head of the Central Cultural Revolution Group. During the Anting Incident he signed to recognize the Workers' General Headquarters as legal, without the consent of the East China Bureau or the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. With this he built his own mass base in Shanghai, and this is also how Wang Hongwen came to his notice. Mao Zedong afterward approved of his “acting first and reporting later.” From 1967 he was chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. He later became a member of the “Gang of Four.” In 1981 he was sentenced to death with a reprieve. He said nothing in court from start to finish.
80: Set up in May 1966. In name it answered to the Politburo Standing Committee. In practice it became the command center of the Cultural Revolution. Chen Boda was head, Kang Sheng adviser, Jiang Qing first deputy head, and Zhang Chunqiao among the deputy heads. Whether it voiced support for a mass organization nearly decided that organization's fate.
82: The East China Bureau of the CCP Central Committee, the leading body the center posted to East China, ranked above the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. During the Anting Incident, both it and the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee held that the Workers' General Headquarters should not be recognized.
84: The demands of the Workers' General Headquarters that Zhang Chunqiao signed his agreement to on the afternoon of November 13, in a dressing room backstage at Culture Square. Pan Guoping and a few Red Guards worked them out on the spot. As recorded by Huang Jinhai, they were as follows. One, recognize the Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters as a legal organization. Two, recognize the November 9 rally and the forced trip to Beijing to petition as revolutionary actions (in similar cases in future, a few representatives will be chosen). Three, the East China Bureau and the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee bear full responsibility for the consequences this time. Four, Cao Diqiu must make a public self-criticism before the masses. Five, give every kind of help to the work of the Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters. The sentence in parentheses is said to have been added by Zhang Chunqiao in his own hand. One hour earlier, at Kangping Road, he had agreed with Tao Zhu, who spoke for the center, that the WGHQ should not be recognized. Two days later in Suzhou, he, Han Zheyi and Cao Diqiu signed another set of Five Demands for Geng Jinzhang's group.
87: A prison in Changping, Beijing, for high-ranking political prisoners. Wang Hongwen was held here after his arrest in 1976. In 1981 he was sentenced to life imprisonment. After 1986 he was moved to a hospital for treatment because of illness. He died of illness on August 3, 1992.
89: A student leader of the Shanghai Red Guard group “Third Headquarters.” He was present at the Anting negotiations and often spoke up for both sides. According to Xie Pengfei, he once talked back to Zhang Chunqiao to his face. He later became a sculptor and changed one character of his name, which is still read Bao Pao. RFA has an interview with him.
91: One of the early core members of the Workers' General Headquarters. He took part in the Anting negotiations, and his memories are one of the main sources on how they went.
93: Born Geng Yuzhang, from Shandong. He had been a private first class in the Nationalist army, was captured in the Jinan Campaign, and at once joined the People's Liberation Army, rising to deputy platoon leader. He joined the Party in 1949, was demobilized to Shanghai in 1957, and worked as a beater operator in a paper mill. In 1964 he was made deputy foreman. After the Anting Incident, about five hundred people who refused to go back chose him to lead them at Kunshan Middle School, because he was a Party member. The “spearhead squad” he organized beat Wang Hongwen when he came to talk them into returning. When they came back from Suzhou he insisted on keeping a list of names and addresses. He then used these four hundred-some people as the base for the “Second Regiment of Workers Returning to Shanghai from the North,” which claimed five or six hundred thousand members. In name it belonged to the Workers' General Headquarters. In fact it did not take orders from Wang Hongwen. Huang Jinhai believed Zhang Chunqiao built up the Second Regiment on purpose to hold the WGHQ in check. After the Commune was founded in February 1967, Geng set up a separate “Great Alliance Committee” to oppose it. Wang Hongwen soon set a trap and had him arrested, and the Second Regiment fell apart. In 1973 Zhang Chunqiao said his error was “splittism” like that of Wang Ming and Chen Duxiu.
96: The article reads, “Citizens of the People's Republic of China enjoy freedom of speech, of the press, of assembly, of association, of procession and of demonstration. The state provides the necessary material facilities to guarantee citizens the enjoyment of these freedoms.” After the Anting Incident, at an enlarged Standing Committee meeting at Diaoyutai, Mao Zedong took out the Constitution and read the passage on “freedom of association.” Speaking to Tao Zhu and Chen Pixian, he asked, “Do workers have freedom of association or not? Do you read the Constitution?” He also said, “On the Shanghai question, Zhang Chunqiao is right. First come the facts, then the policy.” (Wang Rui quoting Wang Li's memoir. Wang Rui dates the meeting to November 16.) This was one of very few moments in the Cultural Revolution when the very top cited the Constitution in public to protect a mass organization. A little over a month later, the same article was not used to protect the Scarlet Guards.
98: A secretary of the Secretariat of the CCP Central Committee's East China Bureau. During the Anting Incident he went to Anting Station, apologized for what the workers had suffered, and promised to send an express train to take everyone to Beijing. When asked, he wrote “Wishing everyone success on the trip north” in a notebook. Then Chen Boda's telegram arrived, and nothing came of it. On the 15th in Suzhou, he, Zhang Chunqiao and Cao Diqiu signed the Five Demands of Geng Jinzhang's group. In the January Storm the rebels seized him to get funds. Huang Jinhai put him and Wei Wenbo up in the Peace Hotel.
100: Head of the dispatch office of the Shanghai Railway Sub-bureau and one of the main leaders of the Scarlet Guards headquarters. According to Huang Jinhai, during the Kangping Road Incident he sent everyone from the dispatch office to Kangping Road, and for a time the railway had no dispatching. He then used trains without authority to send large numbers of Scarlet Guards to Beijing, and Zhou Enlai ordered his arrest. The dispatch document saying the Anting Incident cut the Shanghai-Nanjing line for 31 hours 34 minutes came from his dispatch office.
102: A member of the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee and chairman of the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions. Shortly after two in the morning on November 10, he came out in Cao Diqiu's place to meet the people from the Workers' General Headquarters. He said, “This organization, well, is not in the Sixteen Points,” and refused to recognize it. After he said this, the crowd surged toward North Station. Later, Cao Diqiu signed the Scarlet Guards' Eight Demands, and Chen Pixian passed the Scarlet Guards business on to him and Yang Shifa.
104: Ye Yonglie said that while writing his Biography of Wang Hongwen (《王洪文传》) he found a signed list for bread delivered at Anting on November 10, 1966. While the Municipal Party Committee and the Railway Bureau held the trains, they also sent food to the people on board. Records like this later became one kind of evidence used in the investigations to establish “who had been to Anting.”
113: The big-character poster “Strip Off the Painted Skin and See the Truth.” The title, the date, and the fact of “seven signatures, Wang Hongwen first” follow Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 6, and “Wang Hongwen's First Rebellion,” reposted on the Jiliu website. The text of the poster has not survived and is shown here as blocks of ink. The names of the other six are unknown and are shown as brushstrokes. The one who crossed out his name and signed again is dramatized for the game. Click to enlarge.
122: Sketch map of central Shanghai. Places follow the addresses of the time (311 Yuyuan Road, 274 Hankou Road, the Municipal Party Secretariat on Kangping Road, and others). Rivers and directions are only approximate. Click to enlarge.
129: Zhang Chunqiao signs again in Suzhou
131: Sketch map of the Shanghai-Nanjing line. Distances between stations are drawn to scale from approximate mileage. ⟦0⟧ Click to enlarge.
132: Anting and Kunshan are only one stop apart. In November the rebels were stopped. In December it was the Scarlet Guards.
133: The train was ordered onto a siding at Anting Station at 8:17. See “Anting Incident” on the CPC History website.
136: Zhou Yue'e's ticket. Zhou Yue'e is a fictional character, and the ticket is a game illustration drawn in the usual style of 1960s cardboard tickets. The fare and serial number are not real. The northbound trains stopped at Anting included Beijing-Shanghai express trains. See the first round of fact-checking. Click to enlarge.
139: Chen Boda's telegram. Only sentences quoted in “Anting Incident” on the CPC History website, in Wang Rui's “Rethinking and Re-examining the ‘Anting Incident’,” and in Huang Jinhai's memoir are included. The order of the sentences and the line breaks are guesses. Gray boxes mark text not found in any full version (original text not yet checked). The telegram form is only a sketch and does not copy the original. Click to enlarge.
141: One, recognize the Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters as a legal organization.
142: Two, recognize the November 9 rally and the forced trip to Beijing to petition as revolutionary actions.
143: (In similar cases in future, a few representatives will be chosen.)
144: Three, the East China Bureau and the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee bear full responsibility for the consequences this time.
145: Four, Cao Diqiu must make a public self-criticism before the masses.
146: Five, give every kind of help to the work of the Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters.
148: The Five Demands. The text follows Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》). It is close to the version Wang Rui quotes from “Anting Storm” in Workers' Rebel News (《工人造反报》). Several versions circulated as leaflets at the time. The line in parentheses, in blue, is said to have been added by Zhang Chunqiao in his own hand. The signature is marked only in words, and no handwriting is copied. Click to enlarge.
154:
The No. 17 State Cotton Mill used to be the Japanese-owned Yufeng Cotton Mill. More than eight thousand people, three shifts, machines running 24 hours a day. You worked in the security section. You were in charge of the militia, the gate guards, and the investigations when something went missing in the mill. You earned 64 yuan a month. At home you had your wife, Cui Gendi, and the children.

One day in early June, at noon, the mill's big loudspeakers suddenly began reading out a big-character poster. Nie Yuanzi of Peking University had written a poster that named and criticized the university's Party committee. After that, the loudspeakers read a commentator's article from People's Daily. By the next day word had spread around the mill that Chairman Mao himself had written a comment on it, calling it the first Marxist-Leninist big-character poster in the country.

The canteen went quiet. Someone's chopsticks stopped in midair.

You listened closely. What you thought was this. So the Party committee could be criticized too. So that was what the papers meant.

There were things in the mill that everyone knew about and nobody dared say. Whose relatives got jobs in the mill. Who was named a model worker through connections. Who put his hands on the women workers in the workshop and was never stopped. You were in the security section. You knew more about these things than most.

In those days people in the mill began putting up big-character posters. They were all harmless. They criticized the “Three-Family Village” and figures from history. Nobody touched the factory Party committee.
155: That night, in the dormitory, you found a stack of white paper and started writing.
156:
History The No. 17 State Cotton Mill was formerly the Japanese-owned Yufeng Cotton Mill and had more than eight thousand workers during the Cultural Revolution. Wang Hongwen was then a security officer, earning 64 yuan a month. See Li Xun, “Wang Hongwen, Grassroots Factory Cadre,” in The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 6.

History On June 1, 1966, Central People's Broadcasting Station broadcast the big-character poster by Nie Yuanzi and others. The next day People's Daily printed it in full with a commentator's article. This set off the first wave of big-character posters in factories and schools across the country.

Fiction The canteen scene and Wang Hongwen's thoughts at the time are dramatized for the game.
158: No. 17 State Cotton Mill · Poster board by the clinic
159: Strip Off the Painted Skin and See the Truth
160:
You chose the title of the poster. “Strip Off the Painted Skin and See the Truth.” It was aimed at the factory Party committee.

Seven people signed it, and you signed first. When the other six signed, their hands shook a little. One of them signed, crossed it out, thought for a while, and signed again.

⟦0⟧

As soon as the poster went up, the whole mill was in an uproar. People coming off shift did not go home. They crowded in front of the poster board and read it word by word. Someone read it out in a low voice, and the people next to him nodded. Others read it to the end, said nothing, turned and walked away.

The next day, people from the factory Party committee came to talk to you. They were very polite. They said the masses were welcome to give their opinions, but you should watch your methods and not let bad people use you.

On June 20, a work team sent by the Textile Industry Bureau came into the mill. At the mill-wide workers' and staff congress, the work team named and criticized the leaders of the factory Party committee and said your poster was right. When the meeting broke up, several people who usually kept quiet came over and patted you on the shoulder.
161: You thought the work team had come to support you.
162: June 12　Led the posting of a big-character poster exposing problems in the factory Party committee.
163: June 12　Led the bombardment of the factory Party committee, raising the curtain on the usurpation of power at the No. 17 State Cotton Mill.
164:
History On June 12, the big-character poster “Strip Off the Painted Skin and See the Truth,” drafted by Wang Hongwen and signed by him first, went up with six more signatures after his. It caused an uproar in the whole mill. See the chapter of Li Xun's book reposted on the Jiliu website as “Wang Hongwen's First Rebellion.”

History On June 20, the Party committee of the Textile Industry Bureau sent a work team into the No. 17 State Cotton Mill. At the mill-wide workers' and staff congress it criticized the leaders of the factory Party committee and approved of Wang Hongwen's poster. See RFA, History Across Time (《纵横大历史》), series on the founding of the WGHQ (search summary, original text not yet checked).

Fiction The details of the signing and the people who patted his shoulder are dramatized for the game.
